title: Asia-Pacific markets set for subdued open as investors weigh fresh U.S. tariffs
description: An electronic stock board inside the Kabuto One building in Tokyo, Japan, on Tuesday, Jan. 28, 2025. Toru Hanai | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAsia-Pacific
body: An electronic stock board inside the Kabuto One building in Tokyo, Japan, on Tuesday, Jan. 28, 2025. Toru Hanai | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAsia-Pacific markets were set for a subdued open Thursday as concerns over artificial intelligence spending, sticky inflation and new U.S. tariffs weigh on investor sentiment.Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 57,370 while in Osaka they were last at 57,290 compared with the index's previous close of 57,011.62.Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 22,149 compared with the index's last close of 21,966.01.Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.15%.Focus will be on the implications of a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday, targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.Overnight in the U.S., the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday, advancing 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite, however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday.

schema.headline: Asia-Pacific markets set for subdued open as investors weigh fresh U.S. tariffs

title: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's oil and gas assets outside Russia, sources say
description: Fuel prices at a LukOil gas station in Bloomfield, New Jersey, U.S., on Sunday, March 13, 2022.Gabby Jones | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesInvestors led by
body: Fuel prices at a LukOil gas station in Bloomfield, New Jersey, U.S., on Sunday, March 13, 2022.Gabby Jones | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesInvestors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said. The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said. The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production. The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

schema.headline: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's oil and gas assets outside Russia, sources say

title: Prediction markets push OpenAI IPO expectations later into 2027
description: Attendees arrive for an OpenAI developers conference at Fort Mason on Sept. 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Heather Diehl | Getty ImagesAnthrop
body: Attendees arrive for an OpenAI developers conference at Fort Mason on Sept. 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Heather Diehl | Getty ImagesAnthropic's shaky performance on the public markets since its debut last week and a continuing tech sell-off may be changing the outlook for when prediction markets think OpenAI will go public. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi think there's a roughly 28% chance the ChatGPT developer officially announces an IPO by June 2027. That figure was most recently above 50% earlier this month. Even by October 2027, odds are still only 50-50 that the private company — most recently conducting a funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation — will make its move to the public markets. Kalshi defines officially announcing an IPO as either the Securities and Exchange Commission declaring an S-1 form as effective, the IPO being priced or an exchange has assigned a ticker to the company. Contracts are resolved using reports from media outlets. OpenAI confidentially filed for an IPO in June, but then in an interview with Fortune published in September CEO Sam Altman ruled out a 2026 public markets debut as questions over artificial intelligence safety grew. The company's chief rival, Anthropic, debuted on the public markets last week. However, the stock has declined nearly 30% from its peak during its first trading session, and on Tuesday it closed below its IPO price of $83. Meanwhile, a perpetual futures contract for OpenAI on Hyperliquid has tumbled more than 30% since highs in early October. In late October, OpenAI pared back its goal for its recent funding round to $20 billion from $30 billion. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction markets push OpenAI IPO expectations later into 2027

title: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state
description: Kalshi logo is seen in this illustration taken, August 3, 2026.Dado Ruvic | ReutersUtah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its t
body: Kalshi logo is seen in this illustration taken, August 3, 2026.Dado Ruvic | ReutersUtah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges."Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled."Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X. "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction. The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state

title: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11
description: The Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, center, in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Tuesday, Dec. 6, 2022. Bloo
body: The Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, center, in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Tuesday, Dec. 6, 2022. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesYemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11. The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh. He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack. This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties. Red Sea threatsOn Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.  Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday, according to Reuters. The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25, according to reports.The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet."As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X. The ministry later said two people, a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11

title: Kalshi traders say state data center moratoriums are more likely than not
description: A protester holds a sign that says "Stop Data Centers" during a march to Open AI headquarters in San Francisco, Oct. 20, 2026.Heather Diehl | Getty Im
body: A protester holds a sign that says "Stop Data Centers" during a march to Open AI headquarters in San Francisco, Oct. 20, 2026.Heather Diehl | Getty ImagesOn Wednesday morning, Kalshi traders put the probability above 55% that at least four states would adopt data center moratoriums this year. After Democrats swept Congress and key governor races during the midterm elections, Kalshi traders put the odds that at least four states would pause data center construction at about 75%. Since Nov. 22, the probability that at least four states would adopt moratoriums rose again, to 57% from 52%.The contract asks "How many states will adopt data center moratoriums this year?" and will be verified from state governments. On July 14, New York became the first state to impose a one-year pause on certain state permits for hyperscale data centers. Various local governments have also ordered moratoriums on data centers this year.Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., called for a national data center moratorium the day after the midterms on social media, signaling growing pushback against the build-out. Meanwhile, some investors say unease surrounding the artificial intelligence trade is partly an emotional or sentiment-driven reaction. Doug Clinton, founder and CEO of Intelligent Alpha, told CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime" the AI sell-off is psychological."I actually think it is difficult to point to some fundamental data point from here that all of a sudden would make investors okay," Clinton said. AI-related stocks slumped again Wednesday. Nvidia and Oracle slid more than 8%, while Anthropic tumbled 6% and Alphabet slid 5.5%. On Friday, the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average entered corrections, down 10% from their recent highs, while the Nasdaq Composite declined more than 5% following Anthropic's blockbuster public offering the day before.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Kalshi traders say state data center moratoriums are more likely than not

title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather
description: Workers inflate the Joe Cool and Woodstock balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 in New York City, Nov. 25, 2026.Adam Gray | Getty ImagesMacy's
body: Workers inflate the Joe Cool and Woodstock balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 in New York City, Nov. 25, 2026.Adam Gray | Getty ImagesMacy's on Wednesday announced it's postponing its Thanksgiving Day Parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, due to severe weather.The parade, held each year on Thanksgiving morning, will now take place on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, according to the company. The New York City area is expected to have heavy rain and thunderstorms on Thanksgiving."The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.This year's event marks the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The annual event has never been canceled due to weather, though it was suspended between 1942 and 1944 for World War II.The parade's viability this year had been in question after concerns arose over strong winds that could become dangerous for the massive balloons that the event is known for. Many of the balloons had already been inflated as of Wednesday afternoon. The postponement also means thousands of volunteers and artists slated to perform will have to adapt to Saturday's schedule.

schema.headline: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather

title: Crypto talent will return ‘when AI implodes,’ Arthur Hayes says
description: Arthur Hayes, the former chief executive officer of BitMEX, at the Consensus: Invest event in New York, U.S., on Tuesday, Nov. 28, 2017.Michael Nagle
body: Arthur Hayes, the former chief executive officer of BitMEX, at the Consensus: Invest event in New York, U.S., on Tuesday, Nov. 28, 2017.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesStartup talent that has concentrated in artificial intelligence will return to the crypto industry "when AI implodes," according to Arthur Hayes, chief investment officer at Maelstrom Fund."A lot of talent has gone into the AI space, so I definitely think there'll be a resurgence in good founder talent coming back to crypto," Hayes said in an online interview with CNBC on Tuesday.He added that some founders may also return once they "recognize" that their products could eventually be "usurped by Anthropic or OpenAI."The scale and capabilities of the largest frontier AI labs have made it difficult to "build a real AI business," Hayes said, arguing that "most" founders simply "raise a bunch of money and then light it on fire." He expects the AI trade to face "serious headwinds" in the second half of 2027, when leading labs begin confronting sizable bills tied to compute leases and other non-cancelable commitments. Anthropic expects about $451.6 billion in compute and infrastructure obligations through the end of 2030, with roughly $70.7 billion due by the end of September 2027, according to its prospectus."Do they have the money? We're going to find out," Hayes said.Broader enthusiasm around the AI trade has also cooled amid questions about future infrastructure spending. Even exuberance from Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO on Monday proved short-lived, with the shares falling 5.9% on Tuesday and Anthropic dropping below its IPO price four days after its debut. Bitcoin fall might continueThe co-founder of now-shuttered crypto exchange BitMEX also thinks bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continues to fall. The cryptocurrency has shown little sign of recovery after dropping as low as $55,142.16 on Saturday — its lowest level since July.Bitcoin hit an all-time high of $126,279.63 in October last year and traded as high as $97,915.90 in January this year. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBitcoin prices were at an all-time high of $126,279.63 in October last year and were as high as $97,915.90 in January in the year to date.It has now fallen for seven straight weeks — only the third such streak in its history — with crypto exchange Bitfinex attributing the weakness to equity-market sentiment rather than interest-rate expectations.Hayes said he would like to see bitcoin rebound from around $55,000 even as the Nasdaq continues to fall. That divergence, he said, would suggest markets were shifting from a broad sell-off toward pricing in a "reflation" scenario, with the Federal Reserve eventually providing more liquidity.Neither bitcoin nor gold has yet decoupled from the Nasdaq, with Hayes describing the current market moves as a "correlation-led liquidation.""Stuff goes down, you sell crypto first because it's easy, and then you sell everything else," he said. Once that pattern changes, Hayes said he would be interested in owning Zcash, which he described as a "high beta bitcoin" with a greater focus on privacy, as well as ENA, the token of Ethereum-based platform Ethena.Hayes said a bitcoin rally could push up funding rates and futures-basis returns, increasing the income Ethena earns from its hedged crypto positions. That could make USDe, Ethena's synthetic dollar, more attractive and expand its circulation, he said, adding that he expects the ENA token to rise materially."Those are the two things that I'm keeping an eye on, and when I'm ready to pull the trigger on buying risk again, those will be the things we buy a lot of," Hayes said.

schema.headline: Crypto talent will return ‘when AI implodes,’ Arthur Hayes says

title: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
description: watch nowIn a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on in
body: watch nowIn a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.Former Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan, and current Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh.Consolidated News Pictures | Archive Photos | Getty ImagesBottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.Here are some key points:The nominal Fed funds rate was substantially higher in 1995 than it is today. The real, or inflation adjusted, funds rate was a positive 3.75% back then, and it's now at zero. So the Fed was leaning against the dotcom boom. Greenspan just decided not to lean more. Today, at a zero real rate, the Fed could be said to be fueling the boom.Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was substantially lower, right about target at 1.99% (even though there wasn't a formal 2% target then). It's above target now, at 3.8% according to government data published today, and going the wrong way.The current investment boom now is absolutely off the charts compared with the dot-com era. No real comparison. In 1995, spending on information processing equipment rose 15% year over year. In 2025, it was 27%. Looking at the latest data reported today, it grew 60% in the third quarter at an annualized rate. In the second quarter of 1995, it was 18%. Government deficit spending is substantially more stimulative now than it was then. In 1995, the deficit was just 2.2% of GDP. Today, it's 6.2%. Add higher oil prices, higher tariffs and the recent tax cuts and accelerated depreciation on investments, and there's a lot for the Fed to lean against. It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

schema.headline: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike

title: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic falls 78% after warning its finances are ‘critical’ amid soaring fuel costs
description: Norse Atlantic shares plummeted Wednesday after it revealed the company is in a "critical financial situation" as soaring fuel costs amid the Iran war
body: Norse Atlantic shares plummeted Wednesday after it revealed the company is in a "critical financial situation" as soaring fuel costs amid the Iran war strain budget carriers during the winter season.The Norwegian low-cost carrier said its situation is dependent on securing financing for its short-term liquidity needs.The company has had discussions about a potential strategic takeover as well as other options including ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing.Shares were last trading 78% lower."Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," it added.The start of the U.S.-Iran war on Feb. 28 sent jet fuel prices soaring, putting pressure on airlines around the world. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor.Norse, which offers cheap long-haul flights between Europe, North America, Africa, and Asia, said in October that it was forced to fly with reduced capacity that month, due to "prolonged high fuel prices."Norse Atlantic's CEO Eivind Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline didn't have insight that the crisis would have an immediate impact.watch now"Fuel price rose by more than 100% and the beginning of March we had already sold most of our seats for March so it was difficult to overcompensate with higher prices for those few seats left," Roald said. The airline had cancelled all flights to and from Los Angeles at the time due to the cost of jet fuel, impacting over 150,000 passengers. Roald also said Norse cancelled more than 700 flights in total, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers.The company said in August that geopolitical disruptions and higher jet fuel costs hit profitability in the first half of the year. Higher fuel costs, lower aircraft use, and operational disruptions led to an $8.4 million second-quarter loss, measured before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, and rent. Low-cost carriers struggleEasyJet, another low-cost airline impacted by high fuel costs, reported Wednesday that profit before tax slumped 89% to £71 million ($92.7 million) for the year ending in September 2026. Revenue growth was unable to offset the impact of an 11% increase in fuel costs due to the Middle East conflict, the company said. Earlier this year, Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC  that other European carriers would struggle if jet fuel prices continued to soar. "I think there will be failures." watch now"If it continues at $150 a barrel into July, August, September, then you'll see European airlines fail and that, in the medium term, would probably be good for Ryanair's business."Meanwhile, Ryanair's chief financial officer Neil Sorahan told CNBC in May: "I think we will see some of the weaker carriers who were already struggling before the war possibly go to the wall in the winter." Several smaller European airlines have stopped flying this winter. Slovakia's AirExplore ceased operations, Ireland's Fly4 entered provisional liquidation, and Spain's AlbaStar suspended flights while seeking creditor protection.Spain's Plus Ultra has also suspended all flights while it restructures, though it has not confirmed a permanent closure.

schema.headline: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic falls 78% after warning its finances are ‘critical’ amid soaring fuel costs

title: 10-year Treasury yield slides despite sticky inflation data as investors buy bonds for protection
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) during morning trading on Aug. 24, 2026 in New York City.Angela Weiss | AFP | Getty Im
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) during morning trading on Aug. 24, 2026 in New York City.Angela Weiss | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with investors fleeing to bonds for protection after October's personal consumption expenditures price index showed that inflation continued to accelerate. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points lower at 4.866%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which typically moves in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was down more than 2 basis points at 4.65%.The longer-dated 30-year Treasury yield, which tends to track geopolitical events, was more than 3 basis points lower at 5.254%.One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation — rose 3.8% year over year for October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Separately, economic growth came in much stronger for the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate.The data reinforced expectations for another Fed rate hike in December. "[I]t is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Rate hikes are coming. Lots of them. Bet on it. The economy and inflation are literally on fire."Wednesday's drop comes after yields steadied on Tuesday, with traders digesting softer demand for a 5-year Treasury auction.  Trading is shortened this week due to the Thanksgiving holiday. Bond markets will be closed all day Thursday for Thanksgiving, and will close at 2 p.m. E.T. on Friday.— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed reporting.

schema.headline: 10-year Treasury yield slides despite sticky inflation data as investors buy bonds for protection

title: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
description: Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang arrives for a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Dec. 3, 2025.Evely
body: Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang arrives for a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Dec. 3, 2025.Evelyn Hockstein | ReutersVice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation. "I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation."Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done. Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws."They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO. Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation. "What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe.Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors said it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement.Huang resigned following The New York Times reporting multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed. The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws. "The product they create is a very important part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance said, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence.""We actually see this is an opportunity for Nvidia to focus on complying with American export controls, and we think Jensen Huang is going to take that very seriously," Vance continued."We received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation — and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," Vance said. On Tuesday, Trump left the door open to pardon Huang in an interview with the New York Post, but Vance said on Wednesday that the CEO doesn't need one. "I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vance said. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him."Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door interview with House committees about his dealings with Megaspeed on Tuesday. At the same time, Nvidia will hold its annual conference where it showcases new technology in Washington. — Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation

title: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release
description: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. De
body: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeAbdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, has been released from custody, his attorney told CNBC on Wednesday.The confirmation of Alfozan's release came a day after a federal judge in San Francisco said the defendant would be allowed out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite prosecutors' warnings that he posed a serious flight risk.Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.Alfozan was scheduled to be released from detention Wednesday morning at 8 a.m. PT. Shortly before that deadline, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian of the Northern District of California urged the court to maintain Alfozan's detention pending trial, "given the significant risk that the defendant will flee to Saudi Arabia if he is released from custody."In an order posted on the case docket later Wednesday, Judge Vince Chhabria said the court only learned of the government's last-minute bid to block Alfozan's release after he had already been let out.The government's motion "is therefore denied as moot," Chhabria's order stated. The judge set a hearing for Dec. 3 on the bid to revoke the magistrate judge's order releasing Alfozan.Pointing to Alfozan's "ample resources, significant family and professional ties to Saudi Arabia, and few remaining ties to the United States," Missakian had argued in a court filing that the release conditions imposed by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse "are insufficient to safeguard the defendant's appearance for future proceedings in this case."Alfozan "presents a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate," Missakian wrote.His office sought to pause the magistrate judge's release order until a ruling on a motion to revoke it. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Alfozan's release.Tse in a court hearing Tuesday ruled in favor of Rizk's motion for his client's release, which said prosecutors have admitted finding "no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."In a text message to CNBC after that hearing, Rizk said, "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case."But Missakian's filing Wednesday morning pushed back, saying "the government's investigation of this seven-week-old case is ongoing."Prosecutors have so far found "hundreds of audio files" on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, at least one of which involved representatives of a foreign government and many of which involved discussions of what may be trade secrets," according to the filing."To be sure, what the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation, but the absence of that evidence at this point has no bearing" on whether Alfozan is a flight risk, Missakian argued.Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release

title: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value
description: Zheka-boss | Istock | Getty ImagesAs the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand
body: Zheka-boss | Istock | Getty ImagesAs the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.The shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials."I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality."It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.For Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added."It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she said. Roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated."It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she said. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year."Emphasis on valueThe trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation."You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive."And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed said secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones. Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one."I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved."According to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents plan to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.Iannone said he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year."It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said. The era of personalizationFound Boston vintage market at the former SoWa Power Station, March 29, 2026.Matthew J. Lee | Boston Globe | Getty ImagesAt a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too."Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The company's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece. "To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem said — something unique.That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too. "Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds."Larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen said. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date. "There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen said. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue."

schema.headline: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

title: Ukraine tells Putin to ‘stop complaining’ over oil refinery attacks as Russia promises retaliation
description: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow
body: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow on November 6, 2026.Mikhail Metzel | Afp | Getty ImagesUkrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has told Russian President Vladimir Putin to "stop complaining" over attacks on Russian refineries, saying Putin could end Kyiv's strikes on the oil facilities by bringing an end to the Kremlin's nearly five-year-long war.His comments come shortly after Russia's president told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin on Tuesday that Ukraine continues to attack refining facilities despite U.S. President Donald Trump's appeal to refrain from doing so. "I would like to note that retaliatory action from our side is inevitable. Everyone must be aware of that," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency Tass. In September, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran propelled U.S. diesel prices to a record high. Moscow welcomed Trump's push for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russia's diesel-producing facilities at the time. "If Putin doesn't like Ukraine's strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war," Ukraine's Sybiha said Tuesday via social media."If he doesn't want his military vessels hit, he can order an end to the war. Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion. Clearly, he doesn't care about them. Stop complaining. End the war," he added. CNBC could not independently verify the figures.In July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that about 1.4 million Russian troops were killed, wounded or went missing between the start of the full-scale invasion in Feb. 2022 and June 2026, with more than 30,000 casualties a month in the first half of this year.Satellite view of thick black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara Oblast, Russia, on October 30, 2026.Gallo Images | Gallo Images | Getty ImagesUkraine has stepped up attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Putin's prized Crimea bridge, striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port.Kyiv has also targeted Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Ukraine's long-range strikes had disabled more than 55% of Russia's oil-refining capacity, describing this as a "justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on our energy infrastructure."Putin: Fuel supply situation remains 'challenging'Ukrainian drones reportedly struck two major Russian oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight, triggering fires at both facilities. Satellite images published in late October also showed black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in southern Russia following a suspected Ukrainian drone attack.   Putin on Tuesday said Russia's fuel market situation remains "challenging" and called on government officials and oil executives "to continue reacting promptly to the supply-demand relationship for fuel across the whole territory of Russia," according to Interfax.Ukraine's allies have warned the country faces another winter of blackouts and freezing temperatures amid escalating Russian energy strikes.

schema.headline: Ukraine tells Putin to ‘stop complaining’ over oil refinery attacks as Russia promises retaliation
